Comment 1.1.response:
The reviewer is right that nothing in the objective forces the map to behave like a confidence, and
the submitted paper should not have called it calibrated. We now test the claim directly rather
than assert it. Section IX F compares the map against the absolute error of the backbone output
with respect to the clean reference on every test image. The quantity tested is the demand map $u = 1 - c$, the
one the wrapper acts on, and two diagnostics are reported, the rank correlation and the
sparsification error. The answer is that the map does not carry the meaning the
submitted paper claimed. The pooled rank correlation between the map and the backbone error over the
173 test images is minus 0.258, so the map is not merely uninformative but ordered the wrong way.
The sparsification test agrees. Removing the pixels the map ranks as least reliable raises the
remaining error to 1.88 times its starting value, against an oracle ranking that reaches 0.07, so
the sparsification error is 0.776. We do not report an expected calibration error after an affine
fit, because a calibration error presumes the ordering is right and only the scale is wrong, which
is not the case here. We
therefore took the second branch. The component is renamed a learned cooperation map throughout the
paper, the word calibrated is not used of the map anywhere, and Section IX F states that the map predicts where a
correction helps rather than how wrong the backbone is. The map is nevertheless contributing measurably to the result.
Replacing it by a constant lowers the contrast gain from plus 3.71 to plus 2.51 percent and worsens
five of the six clinical measures, which is why we kept it and renamed it rather than removing it. The cooperation term in Section VIII A is the only place the map is trained toward a meaning. It
rewards agreement between the map and the estimated correction potential, so the map is pushed to be
high where the correction has room to act. Whether that coincides with backbone error is exactly
what Section IX F measures.
changes: Section IX F is new, file 07_results.
The map is renamed a learned cooperation map in Sections IV B and VIII and everywhere else it appears, and the word calibrated is removed from the paper.

full table is in the supplementary file. The honest summary is that the six properties are not equally important. The costliest single
removal is the speckle conformity property P5, which takes 3.19 points of the equivalent number of

to noise gain. Removing the local contrast property P2 costs 0.74 points of the speckle gain and
leaves contrast unchanged, at plus 0.12 points. Removing P3 or P6 changes no measure by more than 0.23 points, on the speckle gain for $P_6$, and removing P4 changes no measure by more
than 0.04 points. All numbers above were
recomputed on the selected checkpoint, the seed 0 model of the tissue bounded gate setting at dead
zone 0.6, which is the model Table 3 reports. The earlier version of this study had been run on a
different checkpoint, and we corrected that before quoting it. We have kept all six rather than pruning the three that are close to inert, for a reason we state in
the paper. The properties are the vocabulary of the rule layer and of the explanation shown to the
reader, and a property that rarely changes the output on this test set can still be the one that
fires on a different scanner or a pathological scan. But we say plainly that on PKU37 three of the
six carry almost all of the effect, and that a reader who wants a smaller rule set can drop P3, P4

Comment 1.3.response:
We agree that this is the right question to ask of any method that raises contrast, and the
submitted paper did not answer it. Section IX H is new and measures the risk directly, using the
clean reference that PKU37 provides. Four quantities are reported over the whole test set. The rate at which an edge appears in the corrected image where the reference has none, before and
after correction. The rate rises, from 0.45 percent of pixels for the backbone output to 0.48 percent after correction, an increase on 127 of the 173 images. We report this as a cost rather than presenting it as a null result. The retention of weak structures, defined as structures whose contrast in the reference lies in the
lowest decile, before and after correction. Retention falls, from 40.5 percent to 37.6 percent, on 168 of the 173 images. This is the clearest cost of the method on this test set and we state it in the results and in the limitations. The behaviour inside dark fluid like regions enclosed by tissue, reported as the fraction of the
image they occupy and the mean absolute change inside them. Dark regions occupy 1.6 percent of the image area and the mean absolute change inside them is 0.0022, against 0.0067 over the whole image, so the correction is about three times quieter where a hypodense region carries the finding. The largest change on any single image across the test set, and the shift of the two strongest layer
boundaries. The mean absolute change over the whole image is 0.0067 and the largest change on any single image is 0.0178. The mean absolute shift of the inner limiting membrane goes from 4.73 to 4.38 pixels and of the retinal pigment epithelium from 9.93 to 10.03 pixels, so the first improves and the second is unchanged within the spread across images. Both happened, and we
have done exactly that. The first sentence of Section IX H now states that the correction raises the
invented edge rate and lowers weak structure retention, both by small but significant amounts, and
the limitations name both. We did not soften either, and we did not reselect the model to avoid them,
because the selection criterion was fixed on the validation split before the test set was scored. One structural fact bounds the risk. The gate suppresses change in the dark region, so a boundary can
only be moved by the additive edge branch within that cap. Section X B states plainly that no
clinician read these images and that a reader study is the correct next step.

We also asked whether the criterion that selected the operating point is blind to these two measures, since it scores six clinical measures and fidelity and neither of the safety measures. It is. Measured on the validation split, so that the test split is used once, the setting the criterion ranked second for NAFNet raises weak structure retention from 40.7 to 43.9 percent where the selected setting lowers it to 37.7, and adds less to the invented edge rate. We report this in the limitations and we did not reselect on it, because the criterion was fixed before the test split was scored and changing it afterwards would spend that split twice.

Comment 1.4.response:
The reviewer's question is what led us to the defect described at the start of this letter, and we
answer it in three parts. What the constants were. The weights 1.5 and 2.0 in the submitted paper were the initial values of
learnable parameters that never moved, because the rule layer was saturated and received no
gradient. They were not chosen at all. What they are now. Section V B states the allocation rule in full. The five budgets are fixed by
one identity, that the base ceiling plus the positive budgets equals one and the base floor minus
the negative budgets equals zero, which keeps the allocation inside the unit interval without
clipping and lets the rule weights train. The rule weights themselves are learned, and Section VIII C
says which quantities were selected on validation. Only one is, the fidelity dead zone, together
with the choice of background rule. Whether any of it materially affects the result. Section IX D varies the base level, each rule weight, and the
conjunction, and re evaluates. Across the fourteen variations no measure turns negative. The largest change in any clinical measure is 0.77 points, on contrast, produced by moving the base level to its lowest setting. The budgets are tied by the identity that keeps the allocation inside the unit interval, so they are held fixed and we vary the base level and the two rule weights that carry the allocation, each of which moves the result by less than 0.2 points. Replacing the Lukasiewicz conjunction by the product moves contrast from plus 3.71 to plus 3.54 percent and by the minimum to plus 3.47 percent, with the other five measures within one part in fifty, so the two alternatives do differ but only slightly. We take the first branch and state both sides of it. One constant matters, the base allocation level, and lowering it trades fidelity for contrast in the direction the design predicts. Everything else, including the choice of conjunction, moves the result very little. We say in the paper that this means the result rests on the shape of the rule layer rather than on the particular logic, which is a reassurance about robustness and a limitation on how much the specific fuzzy calculus can be claimed to contribute.
changes: Section V B states the allocation rule and the identity that fixes its budgets, file 04b_properties_allocation.

Comment 2.2.response:
Section X A is new and explains the trade off and when it is worth accepting. The mechanism is not accidental. A denoiser trained on squared error sits at a local optimum of that
error, so any change to its output moves away from that optimum. The wrapper raises contrast and
boundary definition, and those are not free in squared error terms. The question is therefore not
how to avoid the loss but when to accept it. Two things decide that. The first is the size of the
loss relative to the variation between acquisitions. A few tenths of a decibel is smaller than the
difference between two scans of the same eye. The second is whether the quantity that improves is
the one the reader uses. Layer boundary definition and tissue to background separation are what a
grader uses to place a boundary or judge a fluid pocket. On the transformer backbone we owe the reviewer a correction as well as an explanation. Part of the
SwinIR drop in the submitted version was ours. That corrector had been trained against a half
resolution cache of the backbone output and then tested against the full resolution output, and
the two references differ by 1.61 dB. The cache now runs at full resolution. The revised SwinIR
number is therefore not comparable with the submitted one, and the discussion in Section X A
explains the remaining drop by the windowed attention, which smooths aggressively inside a window
and so gives away the most contrast for the correction to restore. The safety layer already provides the control for a deployment that cannot accept any loss.
Tightening the third constraint reduces the admitted change and the output moves back toward the
backbone. The dead zone of the fidelity term is the training time counterpart, and Section VIII C
reports how the result moves with it.
changes: Section X A is new, file 08_discussion.
The SwinIR reference mismatch is stated and corrected, see the opening of this letter.
Section VIII C reports the dead zone as the one tuned fidelity budget.

Comment 3.4.response:
This was a fair criticism, because the submitted paper used the word without defining it. Section
VII A now gives Definition 1 before the theorem and says what the word does not mean here. It is not
stability in the sense of Lyapunov and we claim no fixed point. The definition is Lipschitz stability of the allocation with respect to the vector of the five rule
truth values, in the maximum norm. A small change in the evidence produces a proportionally small
change in the decision, and the constant is the worst case ratio between the two. We chose that
notion because the rule truth values are exactly what shift when the backbone is replaced or the
scanner changes, so bounding the response to them is the property that matters for the transfer
claim. Section IX G then measures the realised ratio on real images against the constant.

Comment 3.5.response:
Section III B is new and states the problem in the standard form. The decision variables are the
wrapper parameters, with the backbone parameters held fixed. The objective is the expectation over
paired data of a weighted sum of five terms, Equation 1, each of which is defined in Section VIII A.
The three constraints are stated and then given formally in Section VI B. The problem is solved by
mini batch stochastic gradient descent with AdamW, which is possible because every logical
connective is replaced by a smooth piecewise linear surrogate. The reviewer notes that optimisation could be well linked to learning, and we have made that link
explicit. The constraints are handled in two ways that the section now distinguishes. During

Comment 3.12.response:
Section IX G is new and tests each theoretical claim of Section VII numerically on the test set, and
Section I B, Section VII B and Section VII C each now point forward to it. Three things are checked. For the stability result, Theorem 1, we perturb the rule truth values by a controlled amount and
measure the ratio of Definition 1, then compare it with the constant of Equation 12 computed from
the trained weights. The constant is 0.5489 and the largest ratio measured over the 173 test images is 0.4679. The constant is exact for the allocation as a function of the rule truth values, so the gap is not slack in the proof. It means the perturbations a real image produces never reach the worst case the constant allows. For the contrast result, Theorem 2, we measure the tissue gain, the background leakage and the ratio
of background standard deviations on every image and report on how many images the hypotheses hold.
The margin condition holds on 139 of the 173 images and the standard deviation ratio condition on 94, a bare majority, with mean ratio 0.976. The two leakage terms have means of minus 0.0007 in tissue and minus 0.0017 in background against a mean absolute change of 0.0067 over the whole image. Their means sit near zero with a long negative tail, so we also report the per image sign, which is what the margin condition depends on. The tissue term is positive on 137 images and the background term negative on 107. Where a hypothesis fails the theorem makes no prediction, and the measured contrast change there is not systematically different in sign, which suggests the conditions are sufficient rather than necessary. We state the failures rather than exclude them. For the safety layer we report how often each of the three constraints fails and which one binds.
Boundary sharpness is not worsened on 104 of the 173 images, reported as a count and not a mean because the per image worst case is what matters for trusting an individual scan. Of the three constraints, the energy constraint and the bounded change constraint hold on all 173 images and only the no sacrifice constraint ever fails, on 38 of them, so it is the binding one. Acceptance needs two of three and no image falls below two, so the layer returns the candidate in full on every test image. We say in the paper that it is therefore a guard whose bound was measured rather than a mechanism shown to intervene. The allocation map itself is also reported, its mean, spread, minimum and maximum, and the fraction
of pixels at either clamp, which is zero by construction after the repair. The map spans 0.556 to 0.793 with mean 0.726 and standard deviation 0.050, and 0.00 percent of pixels sit at either end of the clamp, against every pixel of every image before the repair.

Section IX E now says that this competitor is the same architecture with the same parameter budget and the same objective, trained for the same ten epochs, with the rule layer replaced by a uniform allocation for the whole of training rather than only at test time. It was fitted before the gate search, so it carries the percentile gate and not the tissue bounded gate NAFNet was selected with, which makes it matched in architecture and not in configuration. The paper says so, and the row is labelled uniform allocation, trained. The second and third are classical
operators, unsharp masking and contrast limited adaptive histogram equalisation, with their
strength tuned on the forty image validation subset under the same rule used for our own constants. The lower blocks of Table 3 report all of them. Training with a uniform allocation reaches plus 4.11 percent contrast and plus 11.58 percent tissue contrast index against plus 3.71 and plus 2.42 for the full method, and it pays 0.42 dB of fidelity against 0.17 dB. It is worse on the other three measures, at 0.71 against 1.21 percent on edge preservation, 16.2 against 23.3 on the speckle measure and 5.8 against 10.7 on the signal to noise ratio, so the two are not ordered. The wrapper adds 168630 parameters shared across backbones plus a head whose size follows the width of the feature tensor it reads, giving 175893 trainable in total for NAFNet, 254538 for SwinIR and values between the two for DnCNN and KBNet, against about seven million frozen. Every backbone is fitted on the same 1388 PKU37 pairs for the same ten epochs from the same warm start, so only the wall clock and the seed spread vary.
